### HTML scraping

Does including header content improve predictions? Answer the question and provide quantitative evidence supporting your answer.

For the Preliminary Task #1 we modified the HTML scraping to include the header tags (h1-h6) in addition to the paragraph ones. of 2,140 HTML webpages, 2,068 had additional header words. Post filtering, we find that we used 1,576 observations for training with 395 testing. We compared logistic principal component regression models using the 120 components selected through validation. The paragraph only model achieved a 79.5% accuracy and 0.863 ROC AUC and the paragraph + header model achieved 78.7% accuracy with 0.847 ROC AUC. This is telling that including headers did not improve binary classification performance.

### Bigrams

Do bigrams capture additional information relevant to the classification of interest? Answer the question, **briefly** describe what analysis you conducted to arrive at your answer, and provide quantitative evidence supporting your answer.

For Preliminary Task #2, we were looking at whether bigrams provided additional predictive information beyond individual words. When generating an out of fold predicted log odds on the bass of word logistic principal component regression model, combining them with bigram principal components in a second logistic regression. We compared 0, 10, 20, 40, and 80 bigram components using the validation data. The 40 component model achieved the highest validation ROC AUC 0.880, slightly above the word only baseline of 0.877. However, on the test set adding bigrams decreased accuracy from 79.2% to 78.7% and ROC AUC from 0.863 to 0.858. In essence, we found no clear evidence bigrams improved classification performance.

### Neural net

For Preliminary Task #3, we trained a neural network on the same paragraph text used in Task 1, represented as TF-IDF scores. The architecture was a small feedforward network: a TF-IDF text-vectorization layer, followed by dropout, a dense layer, dropout again, and a final sigmoid output layer for binary classification. We used the Adam optimizer with binary cross-entropy loss, training for up to 25 epochs with early stopping (halting once validation performance stopped improving, typically well before 25 epochs) to avoid overfitting observed with a fixed epoch count.

We experimented with 10 configurations in total: network size (10, 25, and 64 hidden units), dropout rate (0.2, 0.3, 0.5), including bigrams in addition to single words, limiting vocabulary size, and the share of data held out for early-stopping validation. Because neural network training is stochastic, we additionally reran our best-looking configuration four times to check whether its result was reliable rather than a lucky single run.

Across all configurations and repeated runs, test accuracy consistently fell in the 74-80% range (mean approximately 76%) with ROC AUC around 0.80-0.85, and no configuration reliably matched the paragraph-only logistic PCR benchmark from Task 1 (79.5% accuracy, 0.863 ROC AUC). As a sanity check, a ridge logistic regression fit on the same data independently landed at 79.5% accuracy and 0.845 ROC AUC, nearly identical to the PCR result. Two different methods converging on the same accuracy suggests this reflects a genuine performance ceiling for this dataset size (1,577 training pages) rather than an error in the neural network setup -- the tuned PCR model from Task 1 remains the stronger choice for this classification task.

A single-hidden-layer network (5 units) was also fit on the same 120 principal components used in Task 1's PCR model (`results/nn_model.rds`); its test accuracy is not reported here because the exact feature-generation pipeline used to produce those components was not preserved alongside the saved model, so its performance could not be independently reconstructed and verified for this summary.
